documents.citation: Samuel Gompers, Testimony before the U.S. Senate Committee on Education and Labor, 1883. United States Senate Historical Records; also available through the Library of Congress.
documents.excerpt: We do not want any class legislation. What we want is fair play, and we do not want interference, either from the government on the one hand or from monopoly on the other. We simply ask that the working people shall have a chance — a fair field and no favor... We are not asking for charity. We are asking for our rights, as men. If men who wish to sell the labor of their hands are free to combine for the purpose of getting the best price for that labor, then capital also has a right to combine. The question is whether, in practice, combination by capital can be made as effective and as free from reprisal as combination by labor.

documents.citation: New York Factory Investigating Commission, Preliminary Report, Volume I, 1912. Available through the New York State Library and the National Archives.
documents.excerpt: This Commission finds that the present labor law of the State of New York is inadequate to protect those employed in manufacturing establishments... The Commission recommends the enactment of legislation providing: (1) that all factory buildings shall be fireproof in construction; (2) that all exits, stairways, and fire escapes shall be adequate in number and construction; (3) that a working day of not more than 54 hours per week shall be established for women and minors; (4) that labor inspectors shall have authority to close unsafe premises without judicial approval.

documents.citation: Clayton Antitrust Act, Section 6, United States Congress, October 15, 1914. National Archives and Records Administration.
documents.excerpt: The labor of a human being is not a commodity or article of commerce. Nothing contained in the antitrust laws shall be construed to forbid the existence and operation of labor, agricultural, or horticultural organizations, instituted for the purposes of mutual help, and not having capital stock or conducted for profit, or to forbid or restrain individual members of such organizations from lawfully carrying out the legitimate objects thereof; nor shall such organizations, or the members thereof, be held or construed to be illegal combinations or conspiracies in restraint of trade, under the antitrust laws.
